newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Mir crew confident repairs will succeed.
newsitem.headline: New Mir crew confident repairs will succeed.

text.p: The new crew set to leave for the Mir space station in two weeks expressed confidence on Wednesday they could repair damage caused by a serious accident last month.

"We are not worried; it's normal routine work," said Pavel Vinogradov, who as flight engineer will lead efforts to restore lost power to the 11-year-old station and then patch a puncture in its Spektr module.

"The specialists who have worked on these problems have foreseen practically everything that we might encounter," he told Reuters after a news conference with his flight commander Anatoly Solovyov and NASA astronaut Wendy Lawrence.

Mir collided with its resupply ship on June 25, damaging its solar energy system and forcing the crew of two Russians and one American to seal off the 12-metre (40 ft) Spektr module, which was used for scientific experiments.
Vinogradov, 43, and Solovyov are expected to blast off on August 5. On August 20 they will try to reattach Spektr's interior cables, linked to solar panels outside.
"As far as connecting the cables, there are no questions at all, the operation has already been worked out," Vinogradov said at Star City, Russia's training centre for cosmonauts.
Mission Control first became cautious about entrusting the vital repair work to the current crew after commander Vasily Tsibliyev developed stress-related heart trouble.
When a crewman blundered by unplugging a vital computer, causing the station to lose its orientation for more than a day earlier this month, officials decided to entrust the repairs to a fresh crew.
After reconnecting the cables, the new crew plans on September 3 to take a space walk to examine the small hole on the Spektr's exterior. They will then return at a later date to make the repairs.

"The task is fairly difficult, and unique in that no one has done such work in space before, though there were similar repairs on the American station Skylab and on the Salyut," said Solovyov, a veteran of four missions and a total of 456 days in space. "Based on that experience, we hope to complete the task."

Lawrence, 38, a U.S. Navy commander, is scheduled to replace British-American physicist Michael Foale on September 20. She is not expected to perform repair work, but told reporters she was ready to lend a hand.
She said she would remain inside the station during space walks. "As much as I can I want to help my crew, and whatever we need to do during my time on board."
Solovyov also said he will later attempt a manual docking of the Mir with its cargo ship -- the very procedure that caused the current crisis when Mir hit a similar ship in June.
"We will put it under manual control and then attach to it," he said. "For this we have carried out supplementary training, taking into account all the nuances."

Asked if he was daunted by undertaking such significant repairs on his first mission into space, Vinogradov joked: "My commander is going into space for the fifth time, so if you average that out, that's two and a half times for each."
The two Russian cosmonauts who came aboard Mir on February 12 are scheduled to return to Earth on August 14.
